title: Corvus and the Wobbling Cart
markdown:
Corvus lived on Crooked Cobble Street, where the stones had never agreed on a height, and he did not chase shiny things. He built boats. Tiny ones: hulls for puddles after rain, masts thin enough to stand in a teacup without blushing. His mind ran to straight lines and careful angles. A plan without a drawing, he believed, was only a wish with better posture.

Every day he sat at a weathered plank that served as a workbench, the courtyard quiet underneath. Ink smudged his beak. His feathers puffed when a curve of hull refused to behave on paper. He measured twice, then a third time because the second had felt like guessing. A finished sketch went into a tidy stack. An unfinished one stayed under a smooth pebble, as if the pebble might keep the idea from wandering.

Edie the hedgehog visited often, quills rustling like last autumn's leaves. She would sniff the ink, then the wood, then the little boat itself, which Corvus sometimes forgot to do.

"Corvus," she would say, warm as a pocket, "that's a lovely little boat. The mast looks a bit wobbly. Will it take a breeze?"

He nodded without looking up. "The diagram accounts for the air. See the shading? That's the wind doing what I told it. Perfect, on paper."

Once she set a finished boat in a saucer of leftover tea. It floated. It also listed. Corvus adjusted the drawing, not the keel.

Then a swirly gold sign appeared on Bakery Lane, right beside the workshop. The Gilded Doughnut. Monsieur Pâtisserie arrived with a mustache that puffed when praised and éclairs that made people forget their shopping lists. The grand opening was tomorrow morning. The street smelled already of sugar, butter, and a kind of hopeful hurry.

The delivery cart was not gilded. It leaned as if it had heard a rumor and believed it. One big iron wheel groaned at every push, a long metallic complaint. The pastries inside swayed like jelly on a trampoline. A tray of tarts slid, caught itself, and slid again.

The baker pushed. He pulled. He sweet-talked the wood in French that had more feeling than vocabulary. The lean stayed. His mustache drooped like willow after rain.

Corvus, at his dusty window, felt the familiar tug. A drawing. The cart needed a master plan, something with arrows and shaded force.

He dashed to the plank, largest sheet, fresh ink. Counterweights. Stabilizers. A system of pulleys so elegant the cart would be ashamed to tip. He drew a little crow in the corner for scale, then crossed it out because scale was serious.

Edie wandered over, paws sinking into courtyard dust, and watched his beak fly.

"Corvus. That cart just needs another wheel. A smaller one, on the other side."

He barely looked up. "That won't work. The diagram shows a cleverer way. Much more elegant."

She waited. He added a gear.

The drawing grew into a bird's nest of springs and levers. He calculated the lean as a problem of balance, which it was, and then as a problem of brilliance, which it was not. Edie nudged a rolled blueprint with her nose.

"Look at it. It's tipping because it has one wheel. Like standing on one foot until you have to hop."

Corvus was already sketching a special leg that could pop out at the critical moment, a fancy answer to a plain question. He liked the pop-out leg. It had a dotted line.

Afternoon thinned. He mixed a new pot of ink. He labeled arrows. Once he went to the window, saw the cart still leaning, and returned to the paper as if the paper might have improved in his absence. Edie sat in a patch of dust and did not leave. That, too, was a kind of drawing: a line that stayed.

Dusk came down Crooked Cobble Street. Cooling bread drifted from the bakery, warm and ordinary, the smell of a day that had done its work. Corvus sat in a drift of paper. Blueprints. Notes. A pulley drawn so many times the ink had gone shiny. Outside, Monsieur Pâtisserie wrung his hands as if he could squeeze hope out of them. A single tart had given up and leaned against the cart's rail like a tired guest.

Corvus looked at the cart.

He looked at Edie.

He looked at the most complicated sheet. The lines were beautiful. They were also, he saw now, a kind of hiding.

Crickets started up, unhurried. For a moment nobody solved anything. The lane held the bread-smell and the iron-wheel silence and the small fact of a friend who had already said the useful sentence.

"You know, Edie," he said, quieter than his usual precise talk, "sometimes the most complicated diagram is just one that's trying too hard not to say the obvious thing. This cart. It needs another wheel."

A quiet held. The baker looked at the cart, then at Corvus, then at the cart again, as if the second wheel had been there the whole time in the shape of a missing thought.

"Another wheel?" he whispered.

Edie nudged Corvus's ankle. "See?"

They went around to the back of the bakery, where pans lived in towers and a cat of no particular ambition watched from a flour sack. Under a canvas they found a spare wheel: sturdy, a little scuffed, honest as a loaf. Monsieur Pâtisserie bolted it on with the speed of a man who had been waiting for permission to be simple. The iron complained once, then remembered how to be a pair. The wobble stopped. The cart stood. A small cheer went up from the few who had stayed to watch a disaster refuse to happen.

The baker's mustache rose. "Corvus! Your diagrams—they made me think. They made me see it."

Corvus, who still loved a good line on paper, looked at the two wheels side by side. Tomorrow he would draw the opening route: Bakery Lane, then the square, then the hill where tarts liked to slide. He would also, he suspected, walk outside first and look at the thing itself, especially when Edie's quills rustled and she said the sentence he did not want yet.

On the workbench he left a boat sketch with the mast drawn twice: once as a theory, and once a little thicker, the way a friend draws when she has felt the wind. The teacup-boat waited in its saucer. He did not adjust the paper. He touched the keel, very slightly, until the list gave up.
characters: Corvus (quiet crow boat builder), Edie (hedgehog friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
